Austra College acknowledges that students may raise concerns or be dissatisfied with decisions, services,
behaviours or policies affecting their study or welfare. To uphold the principles of natural justice and
procedural fairness, Austra College provides a structured complaints and appeals process that includes
informal resolution, internal review and external review options where required.
Specifically, Austra College ensures that:
All overseas students have access to a documented, free and easily accessible internal complaints
and appeals process, which is outlined in the Student Handbook, on the website and during
orientation
If a matter cannot be resolved informally, students may formally submit a complaint or appeal using
the appropriate form, with assistance from staff if required
Respond to any complaint or appeal the overseas student makes regarding his or her dealings with
the registered provider, the registered provider’s education agents or any related party the
registered provider has an arrangement with to deliver the overseas student’s course or related
services.
Receipt of any formal complaint or appeal will be acknowledged in writing within 2 working days
Assessment of any formal complaint or appeal will commence within 10 working days of lodgement
and will be finalised as soon as practicable
Students are provided with an opportunity to formally present their case and may be accompanied
and assisted by a support person of their choice at no cost during any meeting or hearing
All complaints and appeals are handled in a professional, fair and transparent manner by
appropriately trained and impartial staff
Students are issued with a written statement of the outcome, including detailed reasons for the
decision, at the conclusion of the internal process
A written record of each complaint or appeal, including the outcome and reasons, is maintained
securely and retained for a minimum of two years after the student ceases to be an accepted
student, or longer where required by Austra College’s records management requirements
If the internal process does not resolve the matter to the student’s satisfaction, Austra College will
advise the student within 10 working days of concluding the internal review of their right to access
an appropriate external complaints or appeals process at minimal or no cost and provide the contact
details of the relevant body.

Protecting Your Fees in Australia
As an international student studying in Australia, your tuition fees are protected by the Tuition
Protection Service (TPS)—a government-backed initiative that ensures you won’t be left out-of-
pocket if your education provider can no longer deliver your course
What Is Tuition Assurance?
Tuition Assurance guarantees that if your Austra College:
Closes unexpectedly, or
Stop delivering your course,
you will be offered:
1. A place in a comparable course with another provider, at no additional cost, or
2. A refund of the unused portion of your prepaid tuition fees.
When Does It Apply?
You must be studying on a student visa with a CRICOS-registered provider.
The course must be cancelled or ceased unexpectedly by the provider (not by student
withdrawal).

the course and shall reflect the value of training delivered within a specified period. At no time shall the
learner be required to make any payment more than statutory guidelines which regulate the amount Austra
College is permitted to require a learner to pay, at any time.

acceptable to the learner that reflects the individual learner’s circumstances.
As with all relationships between Austra College and its learners, all discussions and arrangements entered
remain strictly confidential.
Paying by instalments must be arranged with Austra College office within two weeks of being notified of
acceptance into the qualification.

Referencing
Assessments must be your own original work. If you use another person’s ideas, writing or work and do not
acknowledge the original source, you are committing plagiarism. Referencing is a way of showing that you
are engaging with the literature in your subject area without plagiarising.
Referencing serves several important purposes:
Acknowledges sources of information, so you are not accused of plagiarism
Demonstrates the depth and quality of the research you have done
Allows others to locate sources you have used if they wish to know more
A guide to referencing
S O U R C E O F
I N F O R M A T I O N
S H O U L D Y O U P R O V I D E A R E F E R E N C E ?
Books, newspapers, journals,

(published or online)
Yes

parliamentary debates, treaties
Yes
The internet Yes. It is a common misunderstanding that information on the internet
does not need acknowledgement. You should use material found on
the internet with caution, as it may be unreliable or out of date.
TV, radio, scripts Yes. While you are listening, you should note the program name and
the date of broadcast. Sometimes it is possible to obtain a transcript to
check that you have heard correctly.
Videos, films, DVDs Yes. There are specific conventions for referencing visual media.
Lectures It depends. There are three possibilities:

sections.heading: 1. If the lecturer mentions something which is general knowledge,

sections.heading: 2. If the lecturer presents her/his own idea, you should reference

3. If the lecturer presents another author's idea, you should refer to
both sources: the original author, and the lecturer who presents
the idea. However, in most cases, instead of relying upon your
lecturer's reference, it would be more valuable for you to read the
original author yourself.

sections.heading: 2. If the lecturer presents her/his own idea, you should reference

blocks.text: Illustrations, images, artwork,

codes
Yes. You need to acknowledge the source of drawings, photographs,
graphs, designs, tables, programming codes and all other examples of
non-verbal information that you use in your work.
Quotations Yes. In referencing quotes, be careful to use quotation marks, and be
careful not to change any words.
Paraphrases, summaries Yes. When expressing the information or ideas of someone else in
different words or in a briefer form, you must still acknowledge the
source of the information or ideas.
Common knowledge You don't need to provide a reference for common knowledge - that
is, information shared by many people. It is sometimes difficult to
know what is and what is not common knowledge in your field of
study. If you read or hear the same information many times from
different sources, it is probably common knowledge. Common
knowledge usually includes major historical events, famous people
and geographic areas that are known about by educated people
throughout the world, not just in the country in which they occurred.
If the information is not common knowledge, you should provide a
reference. This shows your reader that the idea is held by an expert in
the field. It also demonstrates to your lecturer that you have been
reading academic texts.
Plagiarism
Plagiarism is taking the words, theories, creations or ideas of another person and passing them off as your
own.
Plagiarism can be deliberate – copying a passage from a book or journal or pasting something from the
internet into an assignment without referencing the original source.
You can also commit inadvertent plagiarism which is where you unintentionally repeat some of the
information you have read in the course of your research. You must ensure you do reference all material
that comes from another source so question yourself as to whether you have read the information
elsewhere and go back to your sources to locate the reference.
Plagiarism can also result from not referencing correctly. You must ensure you know how to reference your
work using the style advised by your trainer/assessor.
Consequences of Plagiarism
At Austra College, academic integrity is taken very seriously. This includes how students use Artificial
Intelligence (AI) tools like ChatGPT, Grammarly, QuillBot, or others. All work submitted must reflect your
own understanding, skills, and knowledge. All forms of plagiarism will be taken seriously - deliberate or not!
Plagiarism is a serious issue that can result in failing an assignment, or even having to leave the course.

Submit your own original work

blocks.text: The purpose of Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) is to provide a comprehensive, consistent
framework for all qualifications offered on a national basis in post-compulsory education and training. The
framework aims to encourage lifelong learning.
The Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) attempts to do so by providing individuals with better scope
to progress through the levels of education and training by improving access to qualifications, by more
clearly defining avenues for achievement and by promoting national and international recognition of
qualifications offered in Australia.
AQF Commitment
The AQF makes a specific commitment to flexible, transparent and systematic learning pathways and to the
removal of boundaries between educational sectors.
Lifelong learning implies a dynamic view of education and training, building strong linkages between learning
at different stages of life and in a wide range of settings and partnerships rather than just looking at various
forms of education and training provision in isolation from each other. The departures from existing views of
education and learning are substantial. They involve recognition of a wide range of learning modes,
strengthening the motivation to learn (wide range of learning opportunities, opportunity to combine
classroom learning with learning in work settings etc.), and providing a wide variety of pathways not
constrained by rigid notions of formal education and training.
Many of the goals of the AQF support such an alternative view of education and learning needed
to promote lifelong learning. These goals include:
Bringing together the qualifications issued by the schools, VET and higher education sectors into a
single comprehensive system of titles and standards
Supporting flexible education and training pathways between sectors and lifelong learning
Encouraging parity of esteem between academic and vocational qualifications
Offering flexibility to suit the diversity of purposes of education and training and provide for the
differences in the constitution of the sectors
Encouraging cross-sectoral partnerships
Underpinning national policies, in particular on quality assurance and articulation and credit
transfer.
Graduating from Austra College or another Australian Qualification Framework (AQF) provider can qualify
you for entry to University.

sections.heading: 5. Policy Statement

blocks.text: This policy ensures overseas students can raise and resolve issues in a safe, respectful environment, free from
disadvantage or retaliation. It is a core part of Austra College’s commitment to student welfare, quality
assurance, and continuous improvement.
Austra College values feedback and takes complaints and appeals seriously.
Austra College:
Encourages informal feedback and early resolution where appropriate
Provides a transparent, fair and timely complaints and appeals process
Ensures all decisions are made with procedural fairness
Respects student privacy and protects students from victimisation or retaliation
Maintains appropriate records of all feedback, complaints and appeals
Ensures international students are informed of their right to internal and external appeal pathways at no
cost or minimal cost

sections.heading: 5. Policy Statement

blocks.text: RTO Code. 40336 Page number 113
International students are additionally protected under the National Code 2018 and are provided with written
outcomes, external review options, and information about contacting the Department of Home Affairs where
their enrolment or visa conditions may be affected.
Austra College acknowledges that students may raise concerns or be dissatisfied with decisions, services,
behaviours or policies affecting their study or welfare. To uphold the principles of natural justice and procedural
fairness, Austra College provides a structured complaints and appeals process that includes informal resolution,
internal review and external review options where required.
Specifically, Austra College ensures that:
All overseas students have access to a documented, free and easily accessible internal complaints and
appeals process, which is outlined in the Student Handbook, on the website and during orientation
If a matter cannot be resolved informally, students may formally submit a complaint or appeal using the
appropriate form, with assistance from staff if required
Respond to any complaint or appeal the overseas student makes regarding his or her dealings with the
registered provider, the registered provider’s education agents or any related party the registered
provider has an arrangement with to deliver the overseas student’s course or related services.
Receipt of any formal complaint or appeal will be acknowledged in writing within 2 working days
Assessment of any formal complaint or appeal will commence within 10 working days of lodgement and
will be finalised as soon as practicable
Students are provided with an opportunity to formally present their case and may be accompanied and
assisted by a support person of their choice at no cost during any meeting or hearing
All complaints and appeals are handled in a professional, fair and transparent manner by appropriately
trained and impartial staff
Students are issued with a written statement of the outcome, including detailed reasons for the
decision, at the conclusion of the internal process
A written record of each complaint or appeal, including the outcome and reasons, is maintained securely
and retained for a minimum of two years after the student ceases to be an accepted student, or longer
where required by Austra College’s records management requirements
If the internal process does not resolve the matter to the student’s satisfaction, Austra College will
advise the student within 10 working days of concluding the internal review of their right to access an
appropriate external complaints or appeals process at minimal or no cost and provide the contact
details of the relevant body.
If any internal or external process results in a decision or recommendation in favour of the student,
Austra College will immediately implement the outcome and advise the student of the corrective or
preventive action taken
Students are advised to seek advice from the Department of Home Affairs where the outcome of a
complaint or appeal may affect their visa conditions.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose

blocks.text: To ensure Vocational RTO monitors and manages international student attendance effectively and complies with
visa conditions, as required under Standard 8 of the National Code of Practice 2018. This policy outlines the
requirements and processes to identify, support, and report students at risk of breaching attendance
obligations.

sections.heading: 2. Scope

blocks.text: This policy applies to:
All international students studying on a student visa at Vocational RTO.
Trainers, Assessors, Student Support Officers, and Compliance Officers responsible for monitoring and
reporting attendance.

sections.heading: 3. Definitions

blocks.text: Term Definition
Satisfactory Attendance Minimum 80% attendance over the scheduled course contact hours per study
period.
Unsatisfactory
Attendance Attendance falls below 80%, unless compassionate or compelling reasons exist.
Study Period 6-month academic term (with internal reviews monthly or quarterly).
PRISMS Provider Registration and International Student Management System.
Warning Letter Formal written notice issued when attendance concerns arise.

sections.heading: 5. Policy Statement

blocks.text: RTO is committed to proactively monitoring international student attendance to ensure compliance with visa
conditions and to support academic success and wellbeing.
All international students are required to maintain a minimum of 80% attendance throughout each study period.
To enforce this, Vocational RTO conducts monthly attendance reviews using its Student Management System
(SMS), supported by a structured early intervention and reporting process.
This policy ensures:
Early identification of students at risk of unsatisfactory attendance;
Transparent communication through progressive warnings and interventions;
Opportunities for students to address attendance issues before a report is made to the Department of
Home Affairs;
Full compliance with Standard 8 of the National Code 2018, particularly clauses 8.10–8.22.
Where a student’s attendance falls below 80%, but not below 70%, and they demonstrate satisfactory academic
progress and compassionate or compelling reasons, the RTO may exercise discretion and choose not to report.
Where attendance falls below 70%, and no valid reasons are presented, the student will be issued a Notice of
Intention to Report (NOIR) and may be reported in PRISMS following due process.

sections.heading: Document text

sections.heading: 1. Purpose

blocks.text: The purpose of this policy is to uphold academic integrity within Austra College by ensuring all assessments
submitted by students are their own work and are free from plagiarism, unauthorised AI use, or collusion. This
policy outlines how Austra College monitors, detects, and responds to breaches of academic integrity.

sections.heading: 2. Scope

blocks.text: This policy applies to all VET students, trainers and assessors, academic staff, and administrative personnel
involved in training and assessment.

sections.heading: 3. Definitions

blocks.text: Term Description
Academic Integrity Honest and responsible scholarship.
Plagiarism Presenting someone else’s work or ideas as your own without proper attribution.
Collusion Unauthorised collaboration with another person in preparing work.
AI Misuse Use of artificial intelligence tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Jasper, etc.) to generate content
without disclosure or validation.
Academic Misconduct Any behaviour that undermines the integrity of academic assessment.

sections.heading: 4. Policy Statement

blocks.text: Austra College is committed to ensuring that all assessment work submitted by students is authentic
and meets the requirements of the training package.
Trainers and assessors are required to apply reasonable methods to confirm the authenticity of a
student’s work, including verbal questioning and validation techniques.
Any suspected or confirmed academic misconduct will be managed fairly, consistently, and in line with
natural justice principles.

sections.heading: 5. Methods of Detection and Verification

blocks.text: Hard Copy Assessments: Trainers may select random paragraphs and use online search engines or
plagiarism and AI detection tools (e.g., Copyleaks, GPTZero) to check authenticity.
PP42 – Academic Integrity and Plagiarism Policy
(Including AI)

sections.heading: 5. Methods of Detection and Verification

blocks.text: RTO Code. 40336 Page number 227
LMS Submissions: Submissions via the LMS are checked using integrated detection software such as
Turnitin or Grammarly.
Verbal Validation: During practical assessments or where doubts arise, the trainer must ask verbal
questions to confirm understanding.
Collusion Check: Where multiple students submit very similar work, collusion is investigated.

sections.heading: 6. First and Repeat Offences

blocks.text: First Offence: Student will be informed, provided support and education, and must re-submit or re-do
the assessment.
Repeat Offence: The student may be required to repeat the entire unit and will receive a formal written
warning. Repeated misconduct may result in suspension or cancellation of enrolment.

sections.heading: 7. Student and Staff Responsibilities

blocks.text: Students must:
o Submit original work.
o Avoid using generative AI unless permitted and declared.
o Acknowledge all sources.
Assessors must:
o Validate authenticity using available tools and questioning.
o Keep records of detection activities and outcomes.

sections.heading: 8. Recording and Reporting

blocks.text: All misconduct cases are documented using the Academic Misconduct Record Form.
Records are filed in the student’s academic record.
Serious or repeat misconduct is recorded in the Academic Misconduct Register.

sections.heading: 9. Step-by-Step Procedure

orientation.

Disability supplement
Introduction
The purpose of the Disability supplement is to provide additional information to assist with answering the disability question.
If you indicated the presence of a disability, impairment or long-term condition, please select the area(s) in
the following list:
Disability in this context does not include short-term disabling health conditions such as a fractured leg, influenza, or corrected physical
conditions such as impaired vision managed by wearing glasses or lenses.
‘11 — Hearing/deaf’
Hearing impairment is used to refer to a person who has an acquired mild, moderate, severe or profound hearing loss after learning to speak,
communicates orally and maximises residual hearing with the assistance of amplification. A person who is deaf has a severe or profound
hearing loss from, at, or near birth and mainly relies upon vision to communicate, whether through lip reading, gestures, cued speech, finger
spelling and/or sign language.
‘12 — Physical’
A physical disability affects the mobility or dexterity of a person and may include a total or partial loss of a part of the body. A physical
disability may have existed since birth or may be the result of an accident, illness, or injury suffered later in life; for example, amputation,
arthritis, cerebral palsy, multiple sclerosis, muscular dystrophy, paraplegia, quadriplegia or post-polio syndrome.
‘13 — Intellectual’
In general, the term ‘intellectual disability’ is used to refer to low general intellectual functioning and difficulties in adaptive behaviour, both
of which conditions were manifested before the person reached the age of 18. It may result from infection before or after birth, trauma
during birth, or illness.
‘14 — Learning’
A general term that refers to a heterogeneous group of disorders manifested by significant difficulties in the acquisition and use of listening,
speaking, reading, writing, reasoning, or mathematical abilities. These disorders are intrinsic to the individual, presumed to be due to central
nervous system dysfunction, and may occur across the lifespan. Problems in self-regulatory behaviours, social perception, and social
interaction may exist with learning disabilities but do not by themselves constitute a learning disability.
‘15 — Mental illness’
Mental illness refers to a cluster of psychological and physiological symptoms that cause a person suffering or distress and which represent a
departure from a person’s usual pattern and level of functioning.
‘16 — Acquired brain impairment’
Acquired brain impairment is injury to the brain that results in deterioration in cognitive, physical, emotional or independent functioning.
Acquired brain impairment can occur as a result of trauma, hypoxia, infection, tumour, accidents, violence, substance abuse, degenerative
neurological diseases or stroke. These impairments may be either temporary or permanent and cause partial or total disability or
psychosocial maladjustment.
‘17 — Vision’
This covers a partial loss of sight causing difficulties in seeing, up to and including blindness. This may be present from birth or acquired as a
result of disease, illness or injury.
‘18 — Medical condition’
Medical condition is a temporary or permanent condition that may be hereditary, genetically acquired or of unknown origin. The condition
may not be obvious or readily identifiable, yet may be mildly or severely debilitating and result in fluctuating levels of wellness and sickness,
and/or periods of hospitalisation; for example, HIV/AIDS, cancer, chronic fatigue syndrome, Crohn’s disease, cystic fibrosis, asthma or
diabetes.
‘19 — Other’
A disability, impairment or long-term condition which is not suitably described by one or several disability types in combination. Autism
spectrum disorders are reported under this category.

title: ICT60220 Advanced Diploma of Information Technology in Australia

sections.heading: Introduction

blocks.text: The ICT60220 Advanced Diploma of Information Technology is a nationally recognised vocational education and training (VET) qualification designed for people who want to learn beyond entry-level IT knowledge. An advanced diploma is at AQF Level 6, above a diploma and below a bachelor’s degree. According to the Austra College’s public course information, it may lead to advanced technical, systems, networking, cybersecurity, and business-facing ICT roles. For a 2026 student, this qualification matters because Australia’s technology workforce remains large, digital skills gaps are still affecting employers, and both government and industry data point to ongoing demand for practical digital capability. Jobs and Skills Australia projects total Australian employment to grow by 6.5% over five years and 13.3% over ten years to May 2035, while ACS says digital technology already supports more than one million jobs and contributes nearly $134 billion to the economy.

sections.heading: Introduction > What is the Advanced Diploma of Information Technology?

blocks.text: At the national level, the qualification is coded ICT60220 Advanced Diploma of Information Technology and is listed as current on training.gov.au. The training package says it reflects the role of people working in a range of ICT roles who have significant specialist technical skills, or managerial, business and people-management capability. It is meant for people carrying out complex tasks in specialist areas, often working independently, leading teams or contributing to strategic business direction.

sections.heading: Introduction > Course purpose and outcomes

blocks.text: The national training package describes the course Advanced Diploma of Information Technology as preparation for advanced work across areas such as advanced data management, cybersecurity, full-stack web development, further programming, IT strategy and organisational development, systems development and analysis, and telecommunications network engineering. The learners become job-ready across varied ICT work contexts and develop skills in areas such as networking, including installing, configuring and testing networks and servers in organisations.

sections.heading: Introduction > Who should study this course?

blocks.text: This course is suitable for the learner who wants to move into IT, cybersecurity, system administration, programming, or business analysis at a higher level. You can also enter the low-level jobs with limited or no vocational experience. In practice, that makes the course suitable both for capable new entrants and for working professionals who want to formalise or deepen their skills.

sections.heading: Introduction > Entry requirements

blocks.text: There are no formal entry requirements. However, provider-level admission rules still apply, entry-level simple rules like
Students must be 18 years or older
International students must hold IELTS 5.5 or equivalent English proficiency
Satisfy any additional admission or enrolment conditions set by the training provider

sections.heading: Introduction > Course Duration

blocks.text: Completing this course takes
104 weeks
of delivery, where
77 weeks
are spent on study and
27 weeks
are spent on holidays.Students must spend
20 hours per week
in classroom study.This study commitment helps learners who are especially balancing study with work
or visa-related attendance obligations.

sections.heading: Introduction > Delivery modes and assessment

blocks.text: The course is delivered face-to-face in a classroom-based model of 20 hours per week. Assessments are conducted through a
A combination of written assignments,
oral questioning,
case studies and projects.
This suggests a practical and applied learning model rather than an exam-only evaluation.

sections.heading: Introduction > Fees and Costs

blocks.text: The course fee may vary from one institute to another. The fee is generally split into tuition fees and non-tuition fees (including application fees and material fees).
Roughly, the cost of the
ICT60220 Advanced Diploma of Information Technology
may start from $30,000.

sections.heading: Introduction > RPL and credit transfer

blocks.text: If you have relevant skills, experience, and knowledge in the IT field and want to upgrade yourself by taking this course, you can reduce the duration and fee of the course through RPL(Recognition of Prior Learning). Compared to the fresh learner, for experienced applicants, the course fee and study material cost is less.

sections.heading: Introduction > Units of competency and curriculum

blocks.text: The current national packaging rules require 16 units in total: 6 core units plus 10 elective units. At least 7 electives must come from the prescribed elective list, and up to 3 units may be selected from approved AQF Level 5 or 6 units from other endorsed training packages or accredited courses, provided they remain relevant and do not duplicate outcomes. The six core units are built around both technical and professional capability: critical thinking for complex problem-solving, team effectiveness, workplace cybersecurity awareness, client interaction at the business level, IP, ethics, and privacy in ICT environments, and planning and monitoring business analysis activities in an ICT environment. This core structure blends technical depth with leadership, stakeholder communication and governance. The elective system is where the course becomes highly career-relevant. Training.gov.au lists specialisation pathways in Advanced Data Management, Cyber Security, Full Stack Web Development, Further Programming, IT Strategy and Organisational Development, Systems Development and Analysis, and Telecommunications Network Engineering. The qualification also includes broader elective pools covering areas such as cloud computing, advanced cybersecurity, application and software development, project management, network security, and other work-ready ICT capabilities. Depending on the elective selection and packaging rules, some providers may issue the qualification with a recognised specialisation.

sections.heading: Introduction > Career Pathways and Job Roles

blocks.text: The most credible way to think about job outcomes is to match your elective stream to the occupation group you are targeting.

sections.heading: Introduction > Further study options

blocks.text: After the ICT60220 Advanced Diploma of Information Technology, continue into a Bachelor of Computer Science, Bachelor of Information Technology, or another relevant qualification.

sections.heading: Introduction > Industry demand and future scope in 2026

blocks.text: The outlook is positive, but it is not uniform across every tech job. Jobs and Skills Australia says Australia’s total employment is projected to grow by 961,000 jobs over five years and nearly 2 million over ten years to 2035. In cyber-related work specifically, JSA reported that Database and Systems Administrators and ICT Security Specialists were projected to grow by 14.2% from May 2024 to 2029, more than double the national average growth rate of 6.6%. ACS’s 2025 Digital Pulse research adds that digital technology supports more than one million jobs, that around 150,000 enterprises may be facing significant or severe digital skills gaps, and that Australia will need 54,000 additional people skilled in cybersecurity operations and management by the end of the decade.

sections.heading: Introduction > FAQs > 1. Is this a nationally recognised Australian qualification?

blocks.text: Yes. The qualification is the ICT60220 Advanced Diploma of Information Technology, which is a nationally recognised qualification and listed as current on training.gov.au.

sections.heading: Introduction > FAQs > 2. Is an Advanced Diploma the same as a Bachelor's degree?

blocks.text: No. An Advanced Diploma is AQF Level 6, while a Bachelor’s degree is AQF Level 7. Of course, the Advanced Diploma is a higher-level VET qualification, but not equivalent to a university bachelor’s program.

sections.heading: Introduction > FAQs > 3. Do I need prior IT study or work experience?

blocks.text: Not necessarily required, because learners get to know everything from the basics. But institutes expect limited experience.

sections.heading: Introduction > FAQs > 4. What does the institute ask for at the admission level?

blocks.text: Basically, Austra expects applicants to be 18 or older, and international students need IELTS 5.5 or equivalent.
We offer this course for both domestic and international students.

sections.heading: Introduction > FAQs > 5. How long does the course take?

blocks.text: Austra’s published duration is 104 weeks, including term breaks.

sections.heading: Introduction > FAQs > 6. How is the course delivered?

blocks.text: The course is delivered face-to-face, 20 hours per week, in a classroom-based model.

sections.heading: Introduction > FAQs > 7. How many units do I complete?

blocks.text: The national packaging rules require 16 units in total: 6 core units and 10 elective units.

sections.heading: Introduction > FAQs > 8. Can I specialise in areas like cybersecurity or full-stack development?

blocks.text: Yes. The qualification includes specialisation pathways such as Cyber Security, Full Stack Web Development, Further Programming, Systems Development and Analysis, Advanced Data Management Information, IT Strategy and Organisational Development, and Telecommunications Network Engineering.

sections.heading: Introduction > FAQs > 9. What does the course cost?

blocks.text: Austra’s fee is $30,000 for ICT60220, but applicants should confirm all current tuition and non-tuition charges directly with us before enrolment.

sections.heading: Introduction > FAQs > 10. Can RPL or credit transfer reduce my study load?

blocks.text: Yes. Recognition of prior study, skills or experience may reduce the duration of the course. Usually, the credit transfer is free, and RPL costs AU$150 per unit.

sections.heading: Introduction > FAQs > 11. What can I do after graduating?

blocks.text: You can get into ICT roles like programming, networking, systems administration, database and security operations, or business analysis.

sections.heading: Introduction > Final verdict

blocks.text: The Advanced Diploma of Information Technology in Australia is one of the strongest VET options for students who want an applied, nationally recognised pathway into higher-level ICT work. It combines AQF Level 6 standing, broad technical specialisations, project-based assessment and progression options into further study. For learners who want practical skills in networking, systems, cyber security, software and business-facing ICT, it opens future opportunities. If you want to explore the course in more detail, check the Austra website.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose

blocks.text: To outline when and how a student’s enrolment may be deferred, suspended, or cancelled, whether initiated by
the student or by Austra College, in full compliance with Standard 9 of the National Code 2018.

sections.heading: 2. Scope

blocks.text: Applies to:
All international students on student visas.
All staff responsible for enrolment management.
Both student- and provider-initiated enrolment changes.

sections.heading: 3. Definitions

blocks.text: Term Definition
Deferral Delay in starting the course, before the official commencement.
Suspension A temporary pause in course enrolment after commencement.
Cancellation Termination of the student’s enrolment.
Compassionate or
Compelling
Circumstances

bereavement).
PRISMS System for reporting enrolment changes to the Department of Home Affairs.

sections.heading: 4. Policy Statement

blocks.text: Austra College is committed to managing the deferral, suspension, and cancellation of student enrolments in a
manner that is fair, transparent, and compliant with the Education Services for Overseas Students (ESOS) Act
2000 and the National Code of Practice for Providers of Education and Training to Overseas Students 2018.
This policy ensures that students are provided with clear guidance on how changes to their enrolment status are
assessed and processed, including their right to appeal and how such changes may impact their visa conditions.
1. Documented Process (Clause 9.1): Austra College has and implements a documented procedure for
assessing, approving and recording student-initiated deferrals and suspensions. This includes:
PP51 – Deferral, Suspension and Cancellation of
Enrolment Policy

sections.heading: 4. Policy Statement

blocks.text: RTO Code. 40336 Page number 271
Submission of a formal request using the Deferral, Suspension or Cancellation Form;
Provision of supporting documentation;
Timely assessment by the appropriate staff member;
Written notification of the outcome to the student;
Accurate recording of all decisions in the Student Management System;
Retention of all records for a minimum of two years after the student ceases to be enrolled.
2. Compassionate or Compelling Circumstances (Clause 9.2): Austra College may approve a deferral or
suspension where compassionate or compelling circumstances exist. These circumstances may include, but are
not limited to:
Serious illness or injury supported by a medical certificate;
Bereavement of close family members;
Major personal trauma;
Natural disaster or political unrest in the student’s home country;
Delay in the issuance of a student visa.
All cases are considered individually and assessed based on the evidence provided.
3. Provider-Initiated Suspension or Cancellation (Clause 9.3): Austra College may initiate suspension or
cancellation of a student’s enrolment for reasons that include, but are not limited to:
Misbehaviour by the student (Clause 9.3.1);
Non-payment of required fees as outlined in the written agreement (Clause 9.3.2);
Breach of course progress or attendance requirements as outlined under Standard 8 (Clause 9.3.3).
All such actions are subject to procedural fairness and will not be finalised until the student has been offered the
opportunity to appeal.
4. Notification and Appeals (Clause 9.4): If Austra College intends to suspend or cancel a student’s
enrolment, the following will occur before action is taken:
The student will be informed in writing of the proposed action and the reasons for it (Clause 9.4.1);
The student will be advised of their right to appeal through Austra College’s internal complaints and
appeals process within 20 working days (Clause 9.4.2).
The enrolment will not be altered in PRISMS until the 20-working day appeal period has lapsed or the appeal
process is concluded, unless exceptional circumstances apply (see Clause 9.6).
5. Visa Implications and Reporting (Clause 9.5): If a student’s enrolment is deferred, suspended, or
cancelled:
Austra College will inform the student that they must seek advice from the Department of Home Affairs
regarding the impact on their visa and whether a new visa is required (Clause 9.5.1);

sections.heading: 4. Policy Statement

blocks.text: RTO Code. 40336 Page number 272
Austra College will report the change to the student’s enrolment status via PRISMS in accordance with
Section 19 of the ESOS Act (Clause 9.5.2).

sections.heading: 6. Appeals and Immediate Risk (Clause 9.6)

blocks.text: The suspension or cancellation of a student’s enrolment cannot take effect until the internal appeals process is
completed, except where the student’s health or wellbeing, or the wellbeing of others, is at risk.
In such cases, Austra College may take immediate action and continue to provide the student with the
opportunity to access the appeals process simultaneously.

title: Elevate Your IT Careers Austra College Advanced Diploma

sections.heading: Overview

blocks.text: IT careers in Australia offer strong job security, high earning potential, and clear specialisation paths in cyber security, networking, software development, and systems analysis. An Advanced Diploma of Information Technology — such as the nationally recognised ICT60220 course at Austra College — is an AQF Level 6 qualification designed to move professionals from support-level roles into specialist and leadership ICT positions.

IT careers continue to be among the most resilient and rewarding paths in Australia’s job market. As businesses across banking, healthcare, retail, and government deepen their reliance on digital systems, the demand for skilled ICT professionals keeps climbing. Cybersecurity threats, cloud migration, data management, and network infrastructure all require people who understand both the technical and strategic sides of technology.

If you’re weighing your options for building a long-term future in IT careers, formal qualifications remain one of the most reliable ways to open doors to higher-level roles. At Austra College , the ICT60220 – Advanced Diploma of Information Technology is designed specifically for learners who want to move beyond entry-level support roles and into specialist or leadership positions within the ICT sector.
This guide answers the most common questions about building IT careers in Australia, what this qualification covers, and how it can help you build genuine, long-term expertise in the field.

sections.heading: Why Are IT Careers in High Demand in Australia?

blocks.text: Technology underpins nearly every industry, and Australian employers consistently report ICT skills shortages, making IT careers one of the most stable professional paths available.

Technology isn’t a passing trend — it’s the backbone of nearly every modern industry. That’s what makes IT careers so different from many other professions: the skills you build rarely become obsolete; they evolve

sections.heading: Why Are IT Careers in High Demand in Australia? > Consistent Industry Growth

blocks.text: Australian employers across finance, healthcare, government, retail, and logistics continue to expand their technology teams. According to Jobs and Skills Australia , ICT professionals remain among the country’s most in-demand skilled occupations, with strong projected growth across software, networking, and cybersecurity roles.

sections.heading: Why Are IT Careers in High Demand in Australia? > Diverse Specialisations

blocks.text: Unlike many trades or professions with a single career track, IT careers branch into numerous specialisations, including:
Cyber security and information protection
Full stack web and software development
Telecommunications and network engineering
Systems analysis and business technology strategy
Data management and analytics
This breadth means you can shape your career around what genuinely interests you, rather than being locked into one narrow path.

sections.heading: Strong Earning Potential

blocks.text: As professionals move from support and technician roles into specialist and managerial positions, earning potential increases significantly — particularly for those who hold formal qualifications combined with practical, real-world experience.

sections.heading: What Does an Advanced Diploma of IT Actually Cover?

blocks.text: The ICT60220 Advanced Diploma of Information Technology is a 16-unit, AQF Level 6 qualification (6 core + 10 elective units) covering advanced ICT skills, business analysis, and a chosen specialisation such as cyber security or networking.

Austra College’s Advanced Diploma of Information Technology is a nationally recognised, AQF Level 6 qualification, built for individuals who already have foundational IT knowledge and want to move into more advanced, specialist, or managerial ICT roles.
Core learning areas typically include:
Applying critical thinking to complex technical problems
Managing IP, ethics, and privacy in ICT environments
Interacting with clients and stakeholders at a business level
Planning and monitoring business analysis activities
Leading and managing team effectiveness in technical environments

Depending on the elective pathway chosen, students can specialise in areas such as cyber security, telecommunications network engineering, systems development, or IT strategy and organisational development — meaning graduates leave with both broad ICT competency and a genuine area of depth.

This structure reflects how real ICT teams operate: technical skill alone isn’t enough at senior levels. Employers increasingly want professionals who can also manage projects, communicate with non-technical stakeholders, and think strategically about technology’s role in the business.

sections.heading: Who Should Study This Qualification?

blocks.text: This course suits IT support staff, Diploma graduates, and experienced professionals who want formal recognition and a pathway into specialist or leadership ICT roles.

This Advanced Diploma is best suited to learners who already hold foundational IT knowledge — typically through a Diploma of Information Technology or equivalent industry experience. It’s an ideal next step for:
IT support staff looking to move into specialist technical roles
Diploma graduates wanting to deepen their expertise
Professionals with hands-on IT experience seeking formal recognition
International students building a long-term ICT career pathway in Australia

sections.heading: What Jobs Can You Get After Completing This Qualification?

blocks.text: Graduates typically move into roles such as Network Administrator, Systems Analyst, Cyber Security Officer, IT Project Coordinator, or ICT Business Analyst.
Network Administrator
Systems Analyst
Cyber Security Officer
IT Project Coordinator
Telecommunications Technologist
ICT Business Analyst

From here, many professionals continue building their IT careers by moving into senior technical leadership, project management, or further study — including pathways into related Business courses for those interested in blending technology with organisational leadership.

sections.heading: The IT Career Ladder

rows: IT Support Officer, Help Desk Technician
blocks.text:
Stage | Experience | Typical Roles | Focus
Entry-Level | 0–2 years | IT Support Officer, Help Desk Technician | Troubleshooting, basic systems support
Early Career | 2–4 years | Network Technician, Junior Developer | Applied technical skills, specialisation begins
Advanced / Specialist | 4–7 years | Systems Analyst, Cyber Security Officer | Complex problem-solving, specialist expertise
Senior / Leadership | 7+ years | IT Manager, ICT Business Analyst | Strategy, team leadership, business alignment
An Advanced Diploma is typically the qualification that helps professionals move from the “early career” stage into genuinely advanced, specialist-level roles.

sections.heading: Why Study IT at Austra College?

blocks.text: Austra College is a nationally registered RTO (Code 40336, CRICOS 03187D) delivering ICT training aligned to real industry needs, with campuses in Adelaide, Melbourne, Sydney, and Perth.
Nationally recognised training, verifiable on the national training register maintained by the Australian Government
Industry-relevant course design, aligned to real ICT job requirements rather than outdated theory
Specialisation options, allowing students to focus on cyber security, networking, systems analysis, or IT strategy
Clear progression pathways, with the option to explore Austra College’s broader ICT Courses or complementary Business and Leadership courses
Support for domestic and international students, including guidance consistent with official Study Australia resources

For learners who want their technical training backed by industry-wide standards, it’s also worth understanding how ICT professionals are recognised more broadly in Australia — the Australian Computer Society is the country’s peak professional body for ICT, offering additional pathways for career recognition and professional development beyond formal study.

sections.heading: How to Get Started

blocks.text: Enquire through the Contact Us page to confirm entry requirements and course structure
Review course fees on the fees page
Apply via the Apply Now page for the Advanced Diploma of Information Technology
Choose a specialisation aligned with your career goals, such as cyber security or systems analysis
Build practical experience through coursework, projects, or industry placement opportunities
Progress further by exploring Austra College’s full range of Trade courses in Australia as your career evolves

sections.heading: Conclusion

blocks.text: IT careers offer something increasingly rare in today’s job market: long-term stability paired with constant opportunity for growth and specialisation. Whether your interest lies in cyber security, networking, systems analysis, or IT strategy, an Advanced Diploma provides the structured, industry-aligned foundation needed to move into more advanced, better-paid roles.
If you’re ready to take the next step in your IT career, Austra College’s Advanced Diploma of Information Technology offers a clear, nationally recognised pathway to get there.
Ready to elevate your IT career? Enquire with Austra College today or explore the full ICT Courses range to find your best-fit pathway.

sections.heading: FAQs

blocks.text: Do I need a Diploma before starting the Advanced Diploma of IT?
t’s strongly recommended. Most students enter with a Diploma of Information Technology or equivalent industry experience, which provides the technical foundation this course builds on.
How long does the course take to complete?
Course duration varies by provider and study load, but this qualification is typically delivered over approximately two years of full-time study, including scheduled breaks.
Can I choose a specialisation within the course?
Yes. Depending on elective choices, students can specialise in areas such as cyber security, telecommunications network engineering, systems development, or IT strategy.
Is this qualification recognised nationally?
Yes. It is a nationally recognised, AQF Level 6 qualification, listed on Australia’s official training register.
What kind of roles can I move into after graduating?
Graduates commonly move into roles such as systems analyst, cyber security officer, network administrator, or ICT business analyst, depending on their specialisation.
Why are IT careers considered future-proof?
Because digital transformation, cyber security needs, and data infrastructure demands continue to grow across every industry, IT skills stay relevant even as specific tools and technologies change.

title: Advanced Diploma of Information Technology: Entry Requirements for International Students in Australia

metadata.version_policy: crawl snapshot; upload path is not an effective date

sections.heading: Introduction

blocks.text: International students who Australia is an ideal destination for international students seeking practical, career-focused education in information technology. If you are looking for practical, career-focused education in information technology, then Australia is the right destination.

Students are popularly interested in advanced IT, networking, cyber security, system administration, cloud technology, and ICT project roles, which are delivered in the Advanced Diploma of Information Technology under the national qualification code ICT60220.
This course is designed specifically for learners who want to handle complex IT tasks, work independently, lead teams and contribute to their ICT operations.

If you are an international student, getting into the course isn’t just about meeting the academic requirements. Before you study in Australia, you need English skills, a visa, money, health coverage, and a genuine student status.
This blog will cover the entry requirements for international students who want to study the Advanced Diploma of Information Technology in Australia.

sections.heading: Introduction > What Is the Advanced Diploma of Information Technology?

blocks.text: An advanced diploma in information technology is a vocational education and training qualification that develops higher-level ICT skills. Depending on the provider and specialisations, some of the course topics may include:
Cyber security
Telecommunications network engineering
Advanced networking
Systems administration
Cloud computing
IT project management
Business analysis
Database and systems support
Usually, international students study on a subclass 500 student visa. So they have to choose the provider and courses that are provided only for international students.
On CRICOS, you will find a list of education providers and courses offered by the Australian Government.

sections.heading: Introduction > Entry Requirements for International Students in Australia > 1. Academic Entry Requirements for International Students in Australia

blocks.text: Academic entry requirements vary between education providers.
However, many colleges commonly expect international students to have completed an Australian Year 12 equivalent qualification or a relevant diploma-level qualification.
As this is an advanced diploma, some providers may prefer students with basic or intermediate IT knowledge.”
Students need to check the exact entry requirements listed by their chosen education provider, because each CRICOS-registered college has its own rules.

sections.heading: Introduction > Entry Requirements for International Students in Australia > 2. English Language Requirements

blocks.text: Students from overseas need to show they know English so they can study, communicate and do their assessment.
The minimum English test score for a student visa is IELTS 6.0 or equivalent.
In most cases, students who take ELICOS before their main course need IELTS 5.0 or equivalent, while some foundation programs require IELTS 5.5.
Here are some common English tests you can take:
IELTS Academic
PTE Academic
TOEFL
Cambridge English
Other Home Affairs-approved English tests

Students should always confirm both the provider’s admission requirements and the Department of Home Affairs visa requirements, as the provider may set a higher score than the minimum visa requirement.

sections.heading: Introduction > Entry Requirements for International Students in Australia > 3. Age Requirement

blocks.text: Most international students applying for an Advanced Diploma of Information Technology are expected to be at least 18 years old.
This is a common provider-level requirement, especially for VET courses delivered to international students.
Students under 18 may need additional welfare and accommodation arrangements before a visa can be granted. Home Affairs requires adequate welfare arrangements for student visa applicants under 18.

sections.heading: Introduction > Entry Requirements for International Students in Australia > 4. Digital Skills and LLND Requirements

blocks.text: The course involves technical IT content; students may be required to demonstrate suitable language, literacy, numeracy, and digital skills before enrollment.
This may be done through previous academic records, an internal LLND test, or a pre-training review.

This helps the provider confirm that the student can manage advanced-level learning tasks such as technical documentation, system analysis, ICT project work, troubleshooting, and online learning systems.

sections.heading: Introduction > Entry Requirements for International Students in Australia > 5. CRICOS Registration and Confirmation of Enrolment

blocks.text: International students can study only the courses offered by providers registered on CRICOS.
So, before applying for a student visa, you need a Confirmation of Enrolment (CoE).

The Department of Home Affairs states that evidence of intended study must be provided to make a valid student visa application, and most students must provide a CoE for all intended courses when they apply.
Before enrolling, students should check:
The provider’s CRICOS registration
Advanced Diploma of Information Technology course CRICOS code
Course duration
Campus location
Study mode
Tuition fees
Intake dates

sections.heading: Introduction > Entry Requirements for International Students in Australia > 6. Financial Capacity Requirement

blocks.text: Students may need to show that they have enough funds to cover living costs, tuition fees, travel, and other expenses.

From 10 May 2024, the financial capacity requirement for the primary student visa applicant increased. Additional funds may be required for a spouse, dependent child, school costs, travel, and tuition fees.
Students should prepare financial evidence carefully. This may include:
Bank statements
Education loan documents
Scholarship letters
Income evidence from parents or sponsors
Proof of access to funds
Tuition fee payment receipts
Because financial requirements can change, students should check the latest Home Affairs document checklist before lodging their visa application.

sections.heading: Introduction > Entry Requirements for International Students in Australia > 7. Overseas Student Health Cover

blocks.text: International students must have an Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC) for the full duration of their study in Australia.
Basic OSHC cover:
Doctor visits
Some hospital treatment
Ambulance services
Limited medicines
OSHC does not usually cover everything, such as dental, optical, or physiotherapy, so students may choose additional cover if needed.

sections.heading: Introduction > Entry Requirements for International Students in Australia > 8. Documents Required for Admission and Visa

blocks.text: While exact requirements vary by provider and visa circumstances, international students should generally prepare the following documents:
Valid passport
Academic certificates and transcripts
English test result
Updated resume, if work experience is relevant
Statement of purpose or Genuine Student responses
Confirmation of Enrolment
Financial evidence
OSHC evidence
Passport-size photograph
Visa application documents
Any documents requested by the provider or Home Affairs
Home Affairs provides a Document Checklist Tool to help students identify which documents may be required based on their passport country and education provider.

sections.heading: Introduction > Final Verdict

blocks.text: The Advanced Diploma of Information Technology can be a strong study pathway for international students who want to build advanced ICT skills in Australia. However, entry is not limited to academic eligibility alone. Students must also meet English language requirements, provider admission rules, financial capacity expectations, OSHC obligations, and student visa documentation requirements. Before applying, students should review the provider’s official course page, confirm the CRICOS registration, prepare complete documents, and check the latest Department of Home Affairs visa requirements. A well-prepared application can improve the chances of a smoother admission and visa process.

sections.heading: Introduction > FAQs > 1. What is the minimum qualification required for an Advanced Diploma of Information Technology in Australia?

sections.heading: Introduction > FAQs > 2. Do international students need IELTS for this course?

sections.heading: What are VET courses in Australia?

blocks.text: VET (Vocational Education and Training) is Australia’s national system of practical, industry-linked qualifications delivered by registered training organisations — assessed on units of competency rather than exams. 5.1 million domestic and international students were enrolled in nationally recognised VET in 2025 (NCVER).

sections.heading: What are VET courses in Australia? > Nationally recognised

blocks.text: A qualification earned in Perth is valid in Brisbane, Darwin or Hobart. Course codes (SIT, CPC, AUR, ICT, BSB, MSF) are set nationally, not by individual colleges.

sections.heading: What are VET courses in Australia? > AQF-aligned

blocks.text: Each qualification sits at a defined level on the Australian Qualifications Framework — Certificate III (AQF 3) through to Graduate Diploma (AQF 8).

sections.heading: What are VET courses in Australia? > Regulated

blocks.text: RTOs are audited by the Australian Skills Quality Authority (ASQA). Courses delivered to international students must also be registered on CRICOS.

sections.heading: What’s the difference between a VET course and a trade course?

blocks.text: Every trade course is a VET course, but not every VET course is a trade course. Trade courses in Australia train you for a specific hands-on occupation — carpenter, chef, motor mechanic, roof plumber, cabinet maker, bricklayer — typically at Certificate III level with substantial practical assessment. A non-trade VET course, like the BSB50420 Diploma of Leadership and Management, builds professional capability without tying you to one on-tools occupation. ELICOS General English sits outside the VET system entirely — it’s a separately regulated English language program, not a nationally recognised VET qualification.

title: Perth Waterproofing Course (CPC31420) – Guide

sections.heading: Overview

blocks.text: A waterproofing course in Perth trains students in the nationally recognised CPC31420 Certificate III in Construction Waterproofing. It covers surface preparation, membrane and coating application, wet-area waterproofing, and workplace safety. Because construction waterproofing sits among the most acute skill shortages in Australia, graduates typically move into paid, in-demand trade roles soon after finishing.
Qualification: CPC31420 – Certificate III in Construction Waterproofing (nationally recognised)
Best for: School leavers, career changers, existing construction workers, and tradespeople who want to specialise
Where you’ll work: Bathrooms, balconies, roofs, basements, external walls, and commercial wet areas

Why now: The Housing Industry Association’s Trades Availability Index placed ceramic tiling — a trade closely linked to wet-area waterproofing — at -0.88 in late 2025, one of the most severe shortages of any trade the index tracks (Austra College, Australia’s Construction Skills Shortage 2026)

sections.heading: Why Trust This Guide?

blocks.text: Skilled trades change fast, so this guide draws on national workforce data, the current Australian Standard for wet-area waterproofing, and published course requirements rather than general impressions. Every figure below is sourced and dated. “If you’re comparing a waterproofing course in Perth, treat this as a starting reference and confirm current fees and intake dates directly with your chosen provider.

sections.heading: What Is Waterproofing in Construction?

blocks.text: Waterproofing is the process of applying protective systems and materials that stop water from entering or damaging a building structure. Buildings face constant moisture exposure from rain, humidity, plumbing, ground water, and everyday household use. Without correct waterproofing, that moisture causes structural decay, mould growth, material breakdown, and expensive repairs.
Waterproofing specialists typically work on:
Bathrooms and wet areas
Balconies
Roof structures
External walls
Foundations and basements
Commercial facilities

The job demands technical knowledge and close attention to detail. Mistakes are costly to fix once tiling, flooring, or other finishes go over the top, so getting it right the first time matters more here than in most trades.

sections.heading: Why Does Waterproofing Matter So Much in Construction?

blocks.text: Waterproofing rarely gets the attention that carpentry or plumbing does, yet it’s one of the most consequential stages of any build. A building’s appearance draws the eye; its long-term performance depends on work most people never see.

It protects buildings from water damage. A skilled waterproofer prepares surfaces correctly, selects the right materials, and applies them to specification, creating a genuine barrier rather than a cosmetic fix.
It’s essential across residential and commercial projects. From apartment blocks to houses to large commercial builds, almost every project needs some form of waterproofing.

It’s a genuinely specialised skill. Waterproofing requires specific knowledge of materials, application methods, and failure points, which is exactly why it works well as a dedicated trade specialisation rather than a generalist add-on.

sections.heading: Why Does Waterproofing Matter So Much in Construction? > Why Choose a Waterproofing Course in Perth?

blocks.text: Western Australia is one of the strongest construction markets in the country heading into 2026. Detached housing approvals and commencements have surged, and WA is forecast to record Australia’s fastest construction growth through 2031 at a projected 4.48% compound annual growth rate, according to Mordor Intelligence’s Australia Construction Market Forecast.

That growth is colliding with a serious labour shortage. Jobs and Skills Australia’s most recent assessment found that every tracked construction trades occupation in Australia is currently classified as being in national shortage — the only industry sector where this is true across the board. Infrastructure Australia separately projects the national construction workforce shortfall will exceed 300,000 workers by mid-2027, up sharply from around 141,000 workers in October 2025.

In Western Australia compounds this further. The state’s historically low unemployment rate, driven heavily by mining and resources, keeps pulling workers away from construction trades. As a result, demand for skilled tradespeople — including waterproofers — has stayed consistently high.
Studying in Perth right now means training for a trade that is:
Practical by nature — you’ll learn to prepare surfaces, apply waterproofing systems, use construction tools correctly, and follow safe work practices in real, hands-on conditions
Genuinely specialised — rather than broad building knowledge, you build deep expertise in one high-demand area
A foundation for long-term progression — a recognised qualification gives you room to keep building experience and expand into related construction work over time.

sections.heading: Why Does Waterproofing Matter So Much in Construction? > What Will You Learn in a Waterproofing Course?

blocks.text: A waterproofing course focuses on the practical and technical skills required for real construction waterproofing work.

sections.heading: Why Does Waterproofing Matter So Much in Construction? > Understanding waterproofing materials:

blocks.text: Different areas of a building need different solutions. You’ll learn about products, application methods, and material preparation so you can make the right call on site rather than just follow a checklist.

sections.heading: Why Does Waterproofing Matter So Much in Construction? > Surface preparation techniques:

blocks.text: Good preparation is arguably the most important part of waterproofing, since most system failures trace back to poor prep rather than poor product. You’ll learn to check surface conditions, prepare areas correctly, and spot problems before installation starts.

sections.heading: Why Does Waterproofing Matter So Much in Construction? > Applying waterproofing systems:

blocks.text: This is where accuracy matters most. Students learn to apply waterproofing membranes, install protective systems, create effective water barriers, and complete tasks to project specification.

sections.heading: Why Does Waterproofing Matter So Much in Construction? > Waterproofing wet areas:

blocks.text: Bathrooms, showers, and laundries are some of the most common — and most failure-prone — waterproofing jobs. The course builds specific skills for these high-frequency scenarios.

sections.heading: Why Does Waterproofing Matter So Much in Construction? > Workplace health and safety:

blocks.text: Training covers safe tool use, handling construction materials, and working safely on active sites, which is essential knowledge for any trade.

sections.heading: > Course Overview: CPC31420 Certificate III in Construction Waterproofing

blocks.text: The CPC31420 Certificate III in Construction Waterproofing is designed for people who want to build specialised waterproofing skills within the construction industry. It’s a nationally recognised qualification under the Australian Qualifications Framework, covering both the core skills common to the construction industry and the specialist field of construction waterproofing.
Through structured training, learners build capability in:
Waterproofing preparation
Applying waterproofing systems
Understanding construction materials
Working with tools and equipment
Following workplace safety procedures

This kind of specialised training gives students a genuine foundation for entering the waterproofing industry — not just a certificate, but a working understanding of how the trade actually operates on site.

sections.heading: Who Should Consider a Waterproofing Course? > School Students:

blocks.text: who enjoy practical work can use waterproofing as a specialised entry point into construction while working toward a recognised qualification.

sections.heading: Who Should Consider a Waterproofing Course? > Career changers:

blocks.text: looking for a practical, hands-on shift may find waterproofing appealing precisely because of how tangible and essential the work is.

sections.heading: Who Should Consider a Waterproofing Course? > Existing construction workers:

blocks.text: can add waterproofing to their skill set, giving them another specialised capability to bring to future projects.

sections.heading: Who Should Consider a Waterproofing Course? > Future trade professionals:

blocks.text: who want to build long-term expertise in a specific, high-demand area of construction may choose waterproofing over broader, more generalist trade paths.

sections.heading: What Career Opportunities After Completing Waterproofing Training?

blocks.text: A waterproofing qualification opens a few different directions within construction:
Waterproofing technician — applying specialised systems to protect buildings from moisture and water-related issues
Construction waterproofing worker — completing waterproofing tasks as part of residential and commercial construction teams
Building maintenance specialist — handling waterproofing repairs and improvements in ongoing maintenance environments
Waterproofing contractor pathway — with experience and any required licensing, some professionals go on to run their own waterproofing services

Pay varies with experience, location, and project scale. National job-ad data from SEEK, compiled by Jora, shows waterproofer roles advertised at an average of roughly $90,000 a year in Sydney and $115,000 a year in Melbourne, while entry-level positions typically start lower and rise with experience and licensing. Treat these as indicative ranges rather than guarantees, since actual pay depends heavily on your employer and location.

sections.heading: What Skills Make a Successful Waterproofing Professional?

blocks.text: Technical training matters, but professionals who thrive in this trade also build specific personal skills:
Attention to detail — waterproofing demands precision, since small mistakes can compromise an entire system
Problem-solving ability — every site presents different challenges that need a practical, on-the-spot solution
Patience and accuracy — careful preparation and consistent application throughout the job
Communication skills — waterproofers regularly work alongside builders and other trades, so clear communication matters
Safety awareness — understanding and following safe work practices on active construction sites

sections.heading: Why Can Waterproofing Be a Smart Career Choice?

blocks.text: It’s essential, not optional. Every quality building project needs protection against moisture damage, so this trade doesn’t go out of fashion.
It blends technical and practical skill. Waterproofers combine material knowledge, process understanding, and genuine hands-on technique.
It offers real variety. The work spans homes, commercial buildings, renovations, and ongoing maintenance.
It supports long-term growth. As you gain experience, you can take on more complex systems and expand your construction knowledge over time.

sections.heading: How to Start Your Waterproofing Career

blocks.text: Research training options. Compare what different waterproofing qualifications actually cover before committing.
Choose a recognised course. A structured, nationally recognised qualification like CPC31420 gives you the depth employers look for.
Complete your White Card. You’ll need general construction induction training before setting foot on most active sites.
Gain practical experience. Hands-on training lets you practise real techniques and build confidence with materials and tools.
Check licensing requirements for your state. Confirm what registration, if any, applies before you start working independently.
Keep learning. Construction methods and materials keep evolving, so ongoing skill development keeps you ready for new opportunities.

sections.heading: Why Choose Austra College for Your Waterproofing Course in Perth?

blocks.text: Choosing the right training provider is one of the most important decisions in starting a construction career. Austra College delivers vocational education and training focused on practical, industry-relevant skills, with a Perth campus and course pathways aligned to trades currently in the most acute national shortage, including construction waterproofing.

For anyone considering a specialised construction trade, the right qualification is the first real step toward a solid professional foundation. It’s also a step into a trade that Australia’s own workforce data shows is genuinely short on skilled people right now.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 1. What is a waterproofing course in Perth?

blocks.text: It’s a vocational training program — built around the nationally recognised CPC31420 Certificate III in Construction Waterproofing — that teaches students waterproofing materials, application techniques, construction practices, and workplace safety.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 2. Why is waterproofing an important construction skill?

blocks.text: It protects buildings from moisture damage and directly affects the durability and long-term quality of residential and commercial structures. Poor waterproofing is one of the most common (and costly) sources of building defects.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 3. What skills are taught in a construction waterproofing course?

blocks.text: Students learn about waterproofing materials, surface preparation, application techniques, wet-area waterproofing, correct tool use, and safe construction practices.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 4. Is waterproofing a good career option in 2026?

blocks.text: Yes — it’s a specialised trade with genuine hands-on work, and it sits within a construction sector where Jobs and Skills Australia currently classifies every tracked trades occupation as being in national shortage, with Western Australia among the strongest construction markets in the country.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 5. Who can study a waterproofing course?

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 6. Where do waterproofing professionals work?

blocks.text: On residential builds, commercial projects, renovations, and maintenance work — anywhere moisture protection is required, which is to say, on almost every construction site.

blocks.text: Waterproofing isn’t the first trade people think of, but it’s one of the most consequential in creating buildings that actually last. A waterproofing course in perth gives you a genuine, nationally recognised qualification, practical hands-on skills, and entry into a specialisation currently in short supply across Australia’s construction industry — backed by real demand data, not just a promising sales pitch.
