title: Light Vehicle Mechanic Salary Australia 2026 – Austra College

metadata.version_policy: crawl snapshot; upload path is not an effective date

blocks.text: A light vehicle mechanic’s pay depends on three things. These are your qualification level, where you work, and who employs you. Apprentices earn award-based rates, and qualified mechanics earn more.
Rates change every year. Always check the current figure in the Fair Work Ombudsman Pay Guide or on Job Outlook.
Many people search “car mechanic salary” before choosing a trade. This guide explains how pay works, what moves it, and how a qualification helps.
Ready to start? Explore the Certificate III in Light Vehicle Mechanical Technology at Austra College.

sections.heading: How Are Light Vehicle Mechanics Paid?

blocks.text: Light vehicle mechanics are usually paid hourly or on a salary.
Under the Vehicle Repair, Services and Retail Award, qualified tradespeople get a minimum wage of 28.12 per hour for Level I and 30.76 for Level II.
Level 1 assistants make less (24.28/hr).
Some employers pay annual salaries (often with superannuation included), while others pay hourly.

sections.heading: Do Mechanics Get Overtime and Penalty Rates?

blocks.text: Weekend and shift work are common in workshops. The award sets higher rates for overtime, weekends, and public holidays. Your exact loading depends on your award, agreement, and hours.
In a busy shop, penalty rates can add up over a year.

sections.heading: How Much Do Apprentice Mechanics Earn?

blocks.text: Apprentices follow a wage scale that rises each year. The award sets the minimum, and some employers pay more. Check current apprentice rates on the Fair Work Pay Guide.
Apprentice wages are lower than a qualified mechanic’s wage. After you finish, you become a qualified tradesperson.

sections.heading: How Much Do Apprentice Mechanics Earn? > Bonuses & Allowances

blocks.text: Bonuses & Allowances
Bonuses are not standard. Some employers offer them, for example for parts or accessory sales.
Some employers pay tool and uniform allowances. Travel or meal allowances may apply if you work on site.

sections.heading: How Much Do Apprentice Mechanics Earn? > Casual Loading

blocks.text: Casual Loading
Casual mechanics usually receive a loading on their base rate instead of paid leave. Check the loading in your award or contract.
A typical pay package includes a base wage, superannuation, allowances and penalty rates. Know your award entitlements before you negotiate.

sections.heading: Factors Affecting Light Vehicle Mechanic Salary

blocks.text: A mechanic’s salary is influenced by a lot of things:

sections.heading: Factors Affecting Light Vehicle Mechanic Salary > Qualifications & Certifications

blocks.text: A trade qualification is the starting point, such as a Certificate III in Light Vehicle Mechanical Technology . Employers usually classify qualified tradespeople at a higher level. Further study can open up diagnostic and senior roles. Heavy vehicle, diesel, and EV work may need extra training or licences.

sections.heading: Factors Affecting Light Vehicle Mechanic Salary > Experience

blocks.text: More years of experience usually bring more responsibility and pay. Strong diagnostic skills help you move into senior roles. Newly qualified mechanics usually start at the lower end of their pay range.

sections.heading: Factors Affecting Light Vehicle Mechanic Salary > Location

blocks.text: Location
Pay varies by region. Remote and mining areas may pay a premium to attract talent. City pay depends on the employer and industry. Compare local job ads with Job Outlook data.

sections.heading: Factors Affecting Light Vehicle Mechanic Salary > Employer Type

blocks.text: Dealerships and major car brands often offer structured training. Smaller or family workshops may pay closer to award rates. Fleet, government and defence roles have their own pay structures. Industry bodies such as the Motor Trades Association and the AMWU can guide you on pay and conditions. Self-employed mechanics set their own rates but have no paid leave.

sections.heading: Factors Affecting Light Vehicle Mechanic Salary > Specialisations

blocks.text: Niche skills are in demand, such as 4×4 tuning, European brands, hybrid and electric vehicles and high-performance engines. Specialists may earn more, depending on the workshop and market.

sections.heading: Factors Affecting Light Vehicle Mechanic Salary > Supply & Demand

blocks.text: Jobs and Skills Australia tracks demand for motor mechanics. When skilled workers are scarce, employers may offer above-award pay to keep staff.

sections.heading: Salary Milestones

blocks.text: Salary Milestones
Most mechanics start as apprentices, then become technicians, senior technicians, and foremen or managers. As you move up, your responsibilities and pay often increase.

rows: Award wage scale while you learn core skills
Higher award rate as your skills grow
Trade classification and more independent work
Complex diagnostics, mentoring, and specialist work
Workshop Manager / Owner Top tier Workshop manager/owner
Business responsibility. Income depends on business performance.
blocks.text:
# | Career stage | What Changes
1 | Apprentice (early years) | Award wage scale while you learn core skills
2 | Apprentice (later years) | Higher award rate as your skills grow
3 | Qualified Mechanic | Trade classification and more independent work
4 | Senior Mechanic | Complex diagnostics, mentoring, and specialist work
5 | Foreman / Leading Hand | Supervisory responsibility
6 | Workshop Manager / Owner Top tier Workshop manager/owner | Business responsibility. Income depends on business performance.

sections.heading: How Can a Mechanic Increase Their Earnings?

blocks.text: Here’s how mechanics can get paid more:

sections.heading: How Can a Mechanic Increase Their Earnings? > Upskill and Certify

blocks.text: Upskill and Certify

More qualifications give you more negotiating power. Options include the Certificate IV in Automotive Mechanical Diagnosis , the Diploma of Automotive Technology and short courses in advanced diagnostics or EV technology. Pay outcomes vary by employer.

sections.heading: How Can a Mechanic Increase Their Earnings? > Specialize

blocks.text: Specialize
Specialists may command higher rates in areas like luxury cars, 4WD, mobile servicing and EV repair, depending on demand.

sections.heading: How Can a Mechanic Increase Their Earnings? > Side Work/Mobile Service ($50–70/hr)

blocks.text: Some mechanics add income through mobile servicing. This brings costs, insurance and tax duties, so seek advice first.

sections.heading: How Can a Mechanic Increase Their Earnings? > Negotiate and Review Pay (5–10% raise)

blocks.text: Review your pay regularly. Compare your rate with Job Outlook data and current job ads before you negotiate.

sections.heading: How Can a Mechanic Increase Their Earnings? > Relocate or FIFO

blocks.text: Relocate or FIFO
Moving to a high-demand region or taking FIFO work may increase earnings. Weigh this against travel, living costs, and time away from home.

sections.heading: How Can a Mechanic Increase Their Earnings? > Gain Experience (~50% claim)

blocks.text: Each year of solid experience builds your skills and your case for a pay review.

sections.heading: How Can a Mechanic Increase Their Earnings? > Running Your Own Business (2–5 years, $120K)

blocks.text: Starting or buying a workshop is a long-term path. It needs business skills and capital. Income depends on your client base and costs, and nothing is guaranteed.

sections.heading: How Can a Mechanic Increase Their Earnings? > Utilise Overtime and Penalties

blocks.text: Utilise Overtime and Penalties
If you can regularly work overtime, the extra pay (1.5–2.5×) effectively boosts your hourly rate. Even one or two Saturdays a month at time-and-a-half can add several thousand per year.

sections.heading: Tax, Super & Entitlements

blocks.text: Tax, Super & Entitlements

sections.heading: Tax, Super & Entitlements > Superannuation

blocks.text: Superannuation

Australian employers must pay super at 12% (the rate since 1 July 2025, and the final scheduled increase) of your ordinary time earnings into a complying fund. A salary package including super is ~10% higher than cash pay. Some workshops allow salary sacrifice into super (or novated car leases) to reduce taxable income.

sections.heading: Tax, Super & Entitlements > Leave and Public Holidays

blocks.text: Leave and Public Holidays

Full-time mechanics get 4 weeks paid annual leave (5 weeks if shiftworker) and paid public holidays. These entitlements translate to ~8–10% extra value beyond gross salary. Apprentices also accrue leave (though first-year juniors may only get school term breaks).

sections.heading: Tax, Super & Entitlements > Overtime Penalties

blocks.text: Overtime Penalties
The award sets penalty rates. Check that your employer pays overtime correctly. You can raise underpayment with the Fair Work Ombudsman.

sections.heading: Tax, Super & Entitlements > Apprentice Support

blocks.text: Apprentice Support
Government incentives for apprentices may apply. Eligibility rules change, so check the Australian Apprenticeships website.

sections.heading: Tax, Super & Entitlements > Tax Implication

blocks.text: Tax Implication

As earnings rise, personal tax increases. However, salary packaging (novated lease for your car, for example) is common among mechanics to save tax. Keep good records for any allowance claims (tools, mobile work).

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > What is the average light vehicle mechanic salary in Australia?

blocks.text: It varies by experience, location and employer. Check Job Outlook for current earnings data.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > How much can an apprentice light vehicle mechanic expect to earn?

blocks.text: Apprentices follow an award wage scale that rises each year. See the Fair Work Pay Guide for current rates.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > Which areas pay the most for mechanics?

blocks.text: Remote and mining regions may pay a premium. Compare local job ads and check allowances.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > What qualifications can boost a Light Vehicle Mechanic salary?

blocks.text: Start with a Certificate III in Light Vehicle Mechanical Technology. Further study, such as a Certificate IV in Automotive Mechanical Diagnosis, can open senior roles.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > Can overtime increase a mechanic’s salary?

blocks.text: Yes. Awards set higher rates for overtime, weekends and public holidays. Your contract sets the exact terms.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > Do casual light vehicle mechanics earn more per hour?

blocks.text: Casuals usually receive a loading instead of paid leave. Your total pay depends on hours and award.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > What are the other benefits for mechanics?

blocks.text: Superannuation, paid leave, and in some jobs tool and uniform allowances.

sections.heading: Conclusion

blocks.text: You earn a trade qualification, such as the AUR30620 Certificate III in Light Vehicle Mechanical Technology. Austra College (RTO 40336) delivers this nationally recognised course. Read our complete guide to becoming a light vehicle mechanic , then view the course page or apply now .

title: What Is a CPC Training Course in Australia? Full Guide

metadata.version_policy: crawl snapshot; upload path is not an effective date

sections.heading: Overview

blocks.text: In the competitive world of construction, obtaining a CPC qualification is a key step in enhancing your career prospects and meeting industry compliance standards. Whether you’re looking to work as a builder, tradesperson, or supervisor, the CPC Training courses are designed to equip you with the skills and knowledge necessary to succeed in Australia’s construction sector. With the rising demand for skilled workers, it’s vital to ensure that your qualifications are up-to-date and meet the requirements set by regulatory bodies.
Did you know?
CPC training is essential for those working in high-risk construction roles.
Learn more about Construction courses
and how they help you meet workplace safety and regulatory standards.

sections.heading: Key Benefits of CPC Courses

blocks.text: The benefits of completing CPC Training Course extend beyond just compliance. Here’s how these courses can positively impact your career:
Industry Recognition: CPC qualifications are nationally recognised, which enhances employability across Australia.
Safety Compliance: The CPC courses ensure workers are trained in industry safety standards, crucial for high-risk environments.
Skill Development: Gain hands-on skills in plumbing, carpentry, building, and other areas of construction.
Career Advancement: Earning a CPC qualification opens the door to higher-level positions and better wages in the construction sector.

sections.heading: Ready to Start Your Construction Career:

blocks.text: Choose the CPC course that matches your career goals and take the first step toward a nationally recognised qualification. Every CPC training course below is delivered by industry-experienced trainers across our Adelaide, Melbourne, Sydney, and Perth campuses.

CPC30220 – Certificate III in Carpentry Master the fundamentals of framing, fitting, and on-site carpentry work — the ideal starting point for a hands-on trade career. Enrol in Certificate III in Carpentry

CPC30620 – Certificate III in Painting and Decorating Learn surface preparation, finishing techniques, and colour application for a career in residential and commercial painting. Enrol in Certificate III in Painting and Decorating

CPC33020 – Certificate III in Bricklaying and Blocklaying Build practical skills in laying bricks and blocks to industry standard, setting you up for a solid trade career. Enrol in Certificate III in Bricklaying and Blocklaying

CPC31420 – Certificate III in Construction Waterproofing Gain specialised training in waterproofing techniques for wet areas, roofs, and below-ground structures. Enrol in Certificate III in Construction Waterproofing

CPC31020 – Certificate III in Solid Plastering Develop hands-on plastering skills for internal and external surfaces, a trade always in demand on construction sites. Enrol in Certificate III in Solid Plastering

CPC50220 – Diploma of Building and Construction (Building) Step up into site supervision and small business building management with advanced construction and compliance skills. Enrol in Diploma of Building and Construction
Not sure which course is right for you? Talk to our course advisors → and we’ll help you find the right pathway for your career goals.

sections.heading: How to Choose the Right Construction Course for You

blocks.text: When selecting a Construction course , it’s important to assess your career goals and the specific qualifications required for your desired job in construction.

sections.heading: How to Choose the Right Construction Course for You > Ask yourself:

blocks.text: What skills do I need?
Which area of construction am I most interested in?
What qualification level is required for my target role?
Working closely with an RTO can help you understand which CPC training course aligns best with your career
aspirations. RTOs play a critical role in providing accurate information to ensure students are enrolled in the
right course for their career path.

sections.heading: What CPC Courses Mean for RTOs

blocks.text: For Registered Training Organisations, delivering CPC Training courses is a critical aspect of ensuring that the construction workforce is skilled, safe, and compliant with the industry’s regulatory requirements. RTOs offering CPC qualifications must stay updated on the latest training packages and regulatory changes issued by the ASQA (Australian Skills Quality Authority) to remain audit-ready. Moreover, RTOs must provide students with relevant resources, training plans, and assessments that align with the national standards for these qualifications.

sections.heading: FAQs > Q1: What does "CPC" stand for, and what does it cover?

blocks.text: CPC stands for Construction, Plumbing and Services — the national training package covering trades like carpentry, bricklaying, plastering, painting, waterproofing, and building and construction management.

sections.heading: FAQs > Q2: Do I need prior experience to enroll in a CPC Training course?

blocks.text: RTOs must ensure all CPC courses are delivered according to the latest training packages and ASQA regulations. Regular audits and reviews of training materials are crucial for maintaining compliance.

sections.heading: FAQs > Q3: How long does it take to complete a CPC course?

blocks.text: Most Certificate III CPC courses run 1 to 2 years full-time, while the Diploma of Building and Construction typically takes around 2 years, depending on your study load and prior credit.

sections.heading: FAQs > Q4: Can international students study CPC courses in Australia?

blocks.text: Yes. CPC courses at CRICOS-registered providers like Austra College are open to international students on a student visa, and many lead to careers in high-demand trades across Australia.

sections.heading: FAQs > Q5: What's the difference between a Certificate III and a Diploma in construction?

blocks.text: A Certificate III (e.g. Carpentry, Bricklaying, Solid Plastering) trains you for hands-on trade work, while the Diploma of Building and Construction prepares you for supervisory or project management roles, including pathways toward a builder’s licence.

sections.heading: FAQs > Q6: Does completing a CPC course lead to a builder's licence?

blocks.text: A CPC qualification is often a required step toward licensing, but licence eligibility also depends on your state’s building authority requirements (e.g. work experience hours). Check with your state regulator alongside your RTO.

sections.heading: FAQs > Q7: What jobs can I get after finishing a CPC course?

blocks.text: Depending on your specialisation, graduates move into roles like carpenter, bricklayer, solid plasterer, waterproofer, painter and decorator, or site supervisor — with strong demand across Australia’s construction sector.

sections.heading: FAQs > Q8: How much do CPC courses cost for international students?

title: How Long Does an Advanced Diploma Take? Time & Pathway Guide

metadata.version_policy: crawl snapshot; upload path is not an effective date

sections.heading: Overview

blocks.text: How long does an Advanced Diploma take? In Australia, it typically takes 18 to 24 months (about 1.5 to 2 years) to complete when studied full-time. Part-time study takes longer, usually stretching to 2.5–3 years depending on the provider and how many units you take per term. This guide breaks down what determines that timeline, how it compares to other qualifications, and what comes next once you finish.

sections.heading: What Is an Advanced Diploma?

blocks.text: Before we get into timing, here’s some quick context if you’re new to the qualification. An Advanced Diploma is a nationally recognised qualification at AQF Level 6, one level above a Diploma and one below a Bachelor’s degree. It’s designed to build advanced, applied skills for complex technical or supervisory work, and — unlike a degree — it’s competency-based rather than research-based, meaning it focuses on demonstrating that you can actually do the work, not just explain the theory behind it. It’s also not a postgraduate qualification — you don’t need a prior degree to enrol; Year 12 completion (or equivalent) is generally enough.

sections.heading: How Long Does an Advanced Diploma Take?

blocks.text: Most Advanced Diploma courses run for 18 to 24 months full-time, split between structured class or workshop time and independent study. At Austra College, for example, both the Advanced Diploma of Information Technology (ICT60220) and the Advanced Diploma of Hospitality Management (SIT60322) run over roughly 18–24 months, combining classroom or workshop-based learning with hands-on training and self-directed study.

So, how long does an Advanced Diploma take compared to the exact figure you’ll see on enrolment paperwork? Providers list it either as a total in months (18–24) or in weeks (roughly 78–104 weeks), which comes down to the same timeframe once you account for term breaks and holidays.

sections.heading: How Does This Compare to a Diploma and Other Qualifications?

blocks.text: A standard Diploma (AQF Level 5) — one level below an Advanced Diploma — usually takes 12 to 18 months full-time. Since an Advanced Diploma builds directly on top of a Diploma’s skill set, many providers structure it as a further 6–12 months of study once you’ve completed the Diploma component, though standalone Advanced Diploma courses (like Austra College’s) are also common and typically run the full 18–24 months.
Here’s how the timelines stack up across the VET qualifications people usually compare:

Qualification | AQF Level | Typical Full-Time Duration
Certificate III | 3 | 1–2 years
Certificate IV | 4 | 0.5–2 years
Diploma | 5 | 1–1.5 years
Advanced Diploma | 6 | 1.5–2 years
Bachelor Degree | 7 | 3–4 years
So, in years, an Advanced Diploma generally takes about 1.5 to 2 years — shorter than a Bachelor’s degree, but a step up in depth (and time) from a standard Diploma.

sections.heading: What Affects Your Timeline?

blocks.text: A few factors can shift your actual completion time either way:

Study mode : Full-time students generally finish in 18–24 months; part-time students often take 2.5–3 years, spreading the same coursework over a longer period. At Austra College, part-time study is available across selected courses, along with weekend, evening, and weekday morning class options — worth confirming directly with our admissions team for your specific course and campus, since availability varies.
Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) : If you’ve got relevant work experience or prior qualifications, you may be able to skip certain units and finish faster.
Study load per term : Taking fewer units per term to balance work or family commitments will naturally extend your timeline.

Practical placement requirements : Some Advanced Diplomas, particularly in hospitality or health-adjacent fields, include supervised placement hours that need to be scheduled around business or industry availability.

Provider-specific structuring : Some providers deliver the Advanced Diploma as a fast 6–12 month top-up for students who’ve already completed the underlying Diploma, rather than the full standalone program.

sections.heading: What Happens After You Finish?

blocks.text: Once you’ve completed your Advanced Diploma, you generally have three realistic paths forward — and each comes with its own timeline implications:

Go straight into the workforce. Advanced Diplomas are designed for job readiness, so many graduates move directly into technical, supervisory, or paraprofessional roles in their field — no further study time needed.

Progress to a Bachelor’s degree with credit. Many universities grant credit transfer or advanced standing to Advanced Diploma graduates, letting them enter a related Bachelor’s degree partway through rather than starting from first year. In practice, this often means the remaining degree takes as little as 1.5–2.5 years instead of the full 3–4, though exact credit varies by university and course — always check the specific articulation agreement before enrolling.

Move into further vocational study. Some students progress into a Graduate Diploma or Graduate Certificate for a specialised area — for example, Austra College’s Graduate Diploma of Management, Learning (BSB80120) is a postgraduate-level option for those who already hold a degree or equivalent experience and want to move into learning and development leadership.

Which path makes sense depends on your career goals, your industry, and whether the roles you’re targeting require a degree by law (as is the case in fields like nursing, teaching, or registered engineering).

sections.heading: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: How long does an Advanced Diploma take? Typically 18–24 months full-time, or 2.5–3 years part-time.
A standard Diploma usually takes 12–18 months, one level below an Advanced Diploma on the AQF.
After completing an Advanced Diploma, most students either enter the workforce, transfer into a Bachelor’s degree with credit, or move into further vocational study.
Your actual timeline can shift based on RPL, study load, placement requirements, and how your provider structures the course.
Austra College’s Advanced Diplomas in IT and Hospitality Management both run 18–24 months full-time across our Adelaide, Melbourne, Sydney, and Perth campuses.

sections.heading: Not Sure Which Timeline Fits Your Life?

blocks.text: Full-time, part-time, fast-tracked with RPL — the right pace depends on your situation. Austra College’s course advisors can map out a realistic timeline based on your background and goals.
Apply Now or contact our admissions team to talk through your options .

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > How long does it take to get a diploma?

blocks.text: A standard Diploma (AQF Level 5) typically takes 12 to 18 months of full-time study, depending on the field and provider.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > How long does it typically take to complete a degree after a diploma or Advanced Diploma?

blocks.text: After a Diploma, credit transfer can bring the remaining degree down to around 2–3 years. After an Advanced Diploma, it can drop as low as 1.5–2.5 years, depending on the university and how closely your course content overlaps with the degree.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > Can I finish an Advanced Diploma faster with credit or RPL?

blocks.text: Potentially, yes. If you have relevant prior study or industry experience, Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) may reduce the time needed to complete your qualification. Confirm your specific eligibility with your provider.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > Does part-time study double the time it takes?

blocks.text: Not quite double, but close — part-time Advanced Diploma study typically takes 2.5 to 3 years, compared to 18–24 months full-time.

title: How to Become a Light Vehicle Mechanic in Australia: A Complete Guide

metadata.version_policy: crawl snapshot; upload path is not an effective date

sections.heading: Introduction

blocks.text: If you are considering a trade career that combines practical employment with contemporary technology, then becoming a light vehicle mechanic in Australia is a great choice. The career role positions fall under the automatic service and repair sector. The most popular way to get started is through an apprenticeship, where you work for a workshop and get paid while completing nationally recognised training through a registered training organisation (RTO). An apprenticeship or traineeship is your training contract with the employer, which must be registered with a state or territorial training authority. And in this blog, you will understand everything about light vehicle mechanics from apprenticeship to salary in Australia.

sections.heading: What is a Light Vehicle Mechanic?

blocks.text: A light vehicle mechanic maintains, tests, diagnoses, and fixes the mechanical system used in light vehicles, including engines, transmissions, suspensions, steering and brakes. This occupation frequently overlaps with the motor mechanic occupation in Australian labour jobs.

Jobs and skills Australia’s occupation profiles describe the core duties of light vehicle mechanic roles, including diagnosing problems, disassembling and removing assemblies, performing planned maintenance, and testing and adjusting the systems after repair.
In the real workshop, your work typically falls into one of the three useful categories:

Routine maintenance and inspection: Conducting regular inspections of vehicle components, such as brakes, tires, and fluids, to ensure everything is functioning properly. This includes performing necessary fluid changes and minor adjustments to keep the vehicle in good working condition.

Diagnosis and repair: Identifying the source of mechanical problems through testing and diagnostic tools, fixing the issue, and then thoroughly testing the repaired system to confirm the solution is effective and the vehicle is safe to operate.
Compliance-related instruction work where mechanics may evaluate cars and provide roadworthiness certificates or identify what work is required to attain roadworthiness.
When comparing light vehicle work with heavy vehicle path, one Australian provider’s summary describes that light vehicle work as up to 4.5 tonnes.

sections.heading: How to become a Light Vehicle Mechanic through an apprenticeship

blocks.text: The most direct pathway to becoming a Light Vehicle Mechanic is an Australian apprenticeship. The apprenticeship model is designed so that you learn in two places at once:
on the job with your employer, and
off the job through structured training with an RTO/TAFE.
The process always begins with employment.
You need an employer willing to take you on as an apprentice.
It could be a
dealership service department,
an independent workshop,
a fleet maintenance team, or a
host employer via a group training arrangement.
After you are hired, there is a training contract you will need to sign and meet state or territory registration requirements, which may vary by state.

The Fair Work Ombudsman says that apprentices and trainees must be registered with the relevant state or territory training authority and that the training contract outlines their rights and responsibilities.
A practical “step-by-step” pathway looks like this:
Get an apprenticeship job offer from an employer.
You will need to sign the training contract and get it approved or registered in your state or territory.
Set up a training plan with the employer and RTO. The training plan is part of a training arrangement negotiated between the employer, apprentice/trainee, and RTO.
Get structured training along with supervised on-the-job training.
Once you have got the skills and qualifications, you can formally finish the apprenticeship.
Note:

It is important to remember that apprenticeships are generally full-time or part-time and not casual. Their pay and entitlements depend on whether they are covered by an award or an enterprise agreement.

sections.heading: Educational requirements to become a Light Vehicle Mechanic

blocks.text: AUR30620 Certificate III in Light Vehicle Mechanical Technology is the benchmark qualification for becoming a light vehicle mechanic.
National Training Register, AUR30620 requires 36 units total: 20 core units and 16 elective units; you can import units from other qualifications (within the rules).
Certificate III courses cover diagnosis, service, and repair across the key systems in light vehicles: the engine, transmission, suspension, steering, brakes, and electrical systems.
There are two common training delivery formats:
Day release: It’s when you go to our training one day a week over semesters.
Block release: You will attend several consecutive training days multiple times during the apprenticeship.
Data from Jobs and Skills Australia shows that most motor mechanics hold a certificate III/IV level qualification, which aligns with the apprenticeship plus certificate III model.

sections.heading: Key skills needed to succeed as a Light Vehicle Mechanic

blocks.text: Light vehicle mechanics need technical skills, but also habits and shop professionalism. Australian occupations emphasise fault diagnosis, dismantling and reassembling components, scheduled maintenance, post-repair testing, and computer-assisted diagnosis. The combination of systematic thinking, mechanical accuracy, and confidence with digital diagnostic tools is what makes a good mechanic. You can boost your employability and earnings potential by learning these skills:

sections.heading: Key skills needed to succeed as a Light Vehicle Mechanic > Diagnostic discipline

blocks.text: This means you confirm the complaint, isolate the system, test methodically, and verify the fix (instead of guessing and swapping the parts).

sections.heading: Key skills needed to succeed as a Light Vehicle Mechanic > Electrical and electronic fundamentals

blocks.text: Wiring diagrams, multimeter usage and scan tool, data interpretation are all the things you need to know these days because many issues involve both mechanical and electronic systems.

sections.heading: Key skills needed to succeed as a Light Vehicle Mechanic > Mechanical precision and clean workmanship

blocks.text: This includes torque procedure, using proper lifting and hoisting techniques, and reassembly/testing once repairs are done.

sections.heading: Key skills needed to succeed as a Light Vehicle Mechanic > Safety mindset and maturity at work

blocks.text: You have to take reasonable care of your own health and safety, follow safety procedures, wear protective gear, attend safety training, and report hazards

sections.heading: Key skills needed to succeed as a Light Vehicle Mechanic > Communication and documentation

blocks.text: The real-time workshop does not only require technical fixes from you. But you also need job cards, clear handovers, and explainable recommendations.

sections.heading: Advancement opportunities for Light Vehicle Mechanics

blocks.text: Opportunity curves don’t end after qualifying. With little specialisation, supervision, or stacking training, a light vehicle mechanic can move into higher-paying and higher-responsible roles.

sections.heading: Advancement opportunities for Light Vehicle Mechanics > Advanced Diagnosis

blocks.text: is a common progression. In some course pathway descriptions,
Certificate III is explicitly positioned as a foundation for further education, whereas
Certificate IV level training and automatic mechanical diagnosis are positioned to enable you to be a problem car expert.

sections.heading: Advancement opportunities for Light Vehicle Mechanics > Inspections and compliance

blocks.text: Here, mechanics are listed as having the ability to inspect vehicles and issue roadworthiness certificates or detailed work needed.
In practice, this kind of responsibility usually comes with additional requirements based on employer and state rules, but it is a recognised path.

sections.heading: Advancement opportunities for Light Vehicle Mechanics > Fleet Maintenance Role

blocks.text: This role is often valued for its reliability, focused thinking and preventive maintenance practices.

sections.heading: Advancement opportunities for Light Vehicle Mechanics > Leadership

blocks.text: If you are a good communicator and help juniors learn safely, the industry is likely to open up senior technician, leading hand, workshop controller, and management style roles.

sections.heading: Final Verdict

blocks.text: In Australia, the light vehicle mechanic part is best understood as a structure burn value learning model:
You get a job,
sign a training contract,
Compplet a certificate III,
learn about the system that makes everyday cars safe.
The apprenticeship guide makes it clear that both employer and apprentice have specific responsibilities around supervision, safety, and training. So you are not left alone guessing.

If you like troubleshooting, want a hands-on career with study demand and want to keep learning as cars get more computerised, then the light vehicle mechanic trade will be your best choice. Because it offers a ladder from apprentice to technician to specialist diagnosis or workshop leader.

sections.heading: Final Verdict > What does a light vehicle mechanic do?

blocks.text: A light vehicle mechanic services, diagnoses, repairs, and tests systems in cars and other light vehicles, including engines, brakes, steering, suspension, and transmissions.

sections.heading: Final Verdict > How do I become a light vehicle mechanic in Australia?

blocks.text: The most common pathway is through an apprenticeship, where you work with an employer while completing structured training through an RTO or TAFE.

sections.heading: Final Verdict > Do I need a qualification to work as a light vehicle mechanic?

blocks.text: Yes. The standard qualification is AUR30620 Certificate III in Light Vehicle Mechanical Technology, which is the main benchmark for entering the trade.

sections.heading: Final Verdict > What is included in a light vehicle mechanic apprenticeship?

blocks.text: An apprenticeship usually includes paid on-the-job training, off-the-job study with an RTO, a training contract, and supervised practical experience in a workshop.

sections.heading: Final Verdict > What skills are important for a light vehicle mechanic?

blocks.text: Key skills include fault diagnosis, mechanical repair, electrical and electronic knowledge, safe work practices, clean workmanship, and good communication.

sections.heading: Final Verdict > How long does it take to become a qualified light vehicle mechanic?

blocks.text: It typically takes the duration of an apprenticeship to complete the required training and workplace experience, depending on the arrangement with the employer and RTO.

sections.heading: Final Verdict > What types of vehicles does a light vehicle mechanic work on?

blocks.text: Light vehicle mechanics generally work on vehicles up to 4.5 tonnes, including standard passenger cars and similar light vehicles.

sections.heading: Final Verdict > How much does a light vehicle mechanic earn in Australia?

blocks.text: The blog notes median weekly earnings of $1,622, around $84,000 annually, with average salaries often ranging from $75,000 to $85,000, depending on experience, location, and employer type.

sections.heading: Final Verdict > Are there career growth opportunities after qualifying?

blocks.text: Yes. Qualified mechanics can move into advanced diagnostics, fleet maintenance, inspections and compliance work, leadership roles, or workshop management.

sections.heading: Final Verdict > Is becoming a light vehicle mechanic a good career choice?

blocks.text: It can be a strong career option for people who enjoy practical work, troubleshooting, and learning new automotive technology, especially as vehicles become more computerised.

sections.heading: Overview

blocks.text: Hospitality management jobs in Australia include restaurant manager, cafe manager, kitchen manager, front office manager, bar manager, club manager, motel manager and catering operations manager — all roles you can pursue after completing the SIT50422 Diploma of Hospitality Management . At Austra College, this nationally recognised diploma runs for 67 weeks (or 24 weeks combined with SIT40521), includes 192 hours of work placement, and is delivered across our Adelaide, Melbourne, Sydney and Perth campuses.
Explore SIT50422 Diploma of Hospitality Management →

Hospitality leadership isn’t just about being good with people — it’s about running a business. Rosters, budgets, compliance, service standards and team performance all sit on a hospitality manager’s desk at once. This guide breaks down the hospitality management jobs available to you, what the SIT50422 qualification actually covers, and how to know if this pathway is right for you.

sections.heading: What Is the SIT50422 Diploma of Hospitality Management?

blocks.text: SIT50422 – Diploma of Hospitality Management is a nationally recognised qualification (CRICOS Course Code: 112998F at Austra College) that develops the operational, leadership and management skills used across the hospitality industry.

It reflects the role of highly skilled senior operators who combine broad hospitality skills with managerial knowledge to coordinate operations. Graduates work independently, take responsibility for others, and make real operational business decisions — not just follow instructions.

The qualification supports multiskilling, with the option to build targeted skills in accommodation services, cookery, food and beverage, or gaming. Everything you learn has to be applied in line with Commonwealth and State/Territory legislation, Australian standards and industry codes of practice.

sections.heading: What Hospitality Management Jobs Can You Get With This Diploma?

blocks.text: Graduates of the SIT50422 Diploma of Hospitality Management at Austra College can pursue hospitality management jobs including:
Banquet or function manager
Bar manager
Cafe manager
Club manager
Executive housekeeper
Front office manager
Gaming manager
Kitchen manager
Motel manager
Restaurant manager
Unit manager, catering operations

These roles span a wide range of employers — restaurants, hotels, motels, catering operations, clubs, pubs, cafés and coffee shops. Completing the qualification does not guarantee immediate employment; outcomes still depend on experience, location, employer demand and individual performance.

sections.heading: What Will You Actually Learn in the Course?

blocks.text: The SIT50422 Diploma covers team management, financial planning, service excellence, compliance and business operations across the hospitality spectrum. This isn’t just about working in hospitality — it’s about running it.

By the end of the course, you’ll be able to lead hospitality teams, manage rosters and budgets, ensure service quality, handle conflict professionally, and run day-to-day operations that keep both guests and the business happy.
To complete the qualification, students finish 28 units of competency — 11 core units and 17 elective units. Core units include
SITXCCS015 – Enhance customer service experiences
SITXCCS016 – Develop and manage quality customer service practices
SITXCOM010 – Manage conflict
SITXFIN009 – Manage finances within a budget
SITXFIN010 – Prepare and monitor budgets
SITXGLC002 – Identify and manage legal risks and comply with law
SITXHRM008 – Roster staff
SITXHRM009 – Lead and manage people
SITXMGT004 – Monitor work operations
SITXMGT005 – Establish and conduct business relationships
SITXWHS007 – Implement and monitor work health and safety practices

Elective units let you specialise — options include food safety, cookery-focused units (working effectively as a cook, preparing meat, seafood and poultry dishes), purchasing goods, making presentations and managing meetings. This flexibility means you can shape the diploma around the specific hospitality management jobs you’re aiming for.

sections.heading: Who Is This Diploma For?

blocks.text: This diploma suits experienced hospitality workers who are ready to move into management and become aspiring leaders — not complete beginners to the industry.

To enrol, you’ll need to be at least 18 years old and have satisfactorily completed Year 11 or higher in your home country. International students also need to meet the college’s English language entry requirements.

Applicants can also qualify through five years of English-medium education in countries including Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the Republic of Ireland, South Africa, the UK or the US, or through prior AQF study on a student visa.

sections.heading: How Is the Course Delivered and Assessed?

blocks.text: The SIT50422 Diploma combines face-to-face classroom training, self-guided learning, theory assessments completed at home, and practical assessment in a simulated workplace environment.

Summative theory assessment happens outside the classroom, while summative practical assessment takes place in Austra College simulated hospitality and kitchen environments — giving you hands-on exposure to real operational systems before you manage them for real.

sections.heading: Does Work Placement Matter for Hospitality Management Jobs?

blocks.text: Yes. Students on the standard 67-week option complete 192 hours of work placement — a genuine opportunity to build practical job skills and gain real industry exposure in an operational commercial kitchen or hospitality setting.

Work placement bridges the gap between classroom learning and the fast-paced reality of hospitality management jobs. Employers consistently look for candidates who’ve already proven they can operate under real service pressure, not just in a simulated classroom.

sections.heading: What Comes After the Diploma?

blocks.text: Graduates can progress into the SIT60322 Advanced Diploma of Hospitality Management to build further strategic leadership and business management skills — the natural next step if you’re aiming for senior operations or ownership roles rather than departmental management.

For those interested in broader leadership capability beyond hospitality-specific operations, it’s also worth understanding the core principles that underpin strong management generally — self-awareness, strategic thinking, relationship building and empowerment — which apply just as much to a restaurant floor as to any other team.

sections.heading: Why Study This Diploma at Austra College?

blocks.text: When you’re choosing where to study your SIT50422 , you’re not just picking a course code — you’re picking who prepares you for the job you actually want.
You’ll learn from people who’ve done the job, not just taught it:

Your trainers have real hospitality management experience, so when you ask about handling a difficult roster or a budget blowout, you’re getting an answer grounded in what actually happens on the floor — not just textbook theory.

You’ll be tested on how you perform, not just what you can write: Between your 192 hours of work placement and practical assessment in Austra College’s simulated hospitality and kitchen environments, you get to prove you can actually run operations under pressure — before you’re doing it for real, with real consequences.

You can study where you plan to work: With campuses in Adelaide, Melbourne, Sydney and Perth, you don’t have to choose between your qualification and your local industry network. You build connections in the city you’re actually going to work in.

You already know what comes next: If you finish this diploma and want to keep climbing, Austra College also runs the SIT60322 Advanced Diploma of Hospitality Management . You don’t have to research a new provider or start your applications from scratch — the next step is already mapped out for you.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 1. What is SIT50422 – Diploma of Hospitality Management?

blocks.text: SIT50422 – Diploma of Hospitality Management is a nationally recognised qualification that develops operational, leadership and management skills for the hospitality industry.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 2. What skills will I learn during the course?

blocks.text: Students develop skills in managing hospitality operations, leading teams, preparing budgets, managing customer service, handling workplace conflict, maintaining business relationships and monitoring workplace safety.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 3. How long does the Diploma of Hospitality Management take?

blocks.text: The standard course duration is 67 weeks, including eight weeks of scheduled breaks and 192 hours of work placement. A 24-week option may apply to eligible students enrolled in the combined SIT40521 and SIT50422 package.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 4. How is the course delivered and assessed?

blocks.text: The course combines face-to-face classroom training, self-guided learning, theory assessments completed at home and practical assessments conducted in a simulated workplace environment.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 5. Does the course include work placement?

blocks.text: Yes. Students completing the standard course option must undertake 192 hours of work placement, allowing them to apply their skills in an operational hospitality environment.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 6. What hospitality management jobs may be available after completing the course?

blocks.text: Graduates may pursue roles such as restaurant manager, cafe manager, kitchen manager, front office manager, bar manager, club manager, motel manager or catering operations manager. Completion of the qualification does not guarantee employment.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 7. Can I continue studying after completing SIT50422?

blocks.text: Yes. Graduates may progress to SIT60322 – Advanced Diploma of Hospitality Management to further develop strategic leadership and business management skills.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 8. Where is the course delivered?

blocks.text: Austra College delivers this diploma in Adelaide, Melbourne, Sydney and Perth. Available facilities and delivery arrangements may vary between locations.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions > 9. Can I apply for credit transfer?

blocks.text: Yes. Austra College recognises AQF Qualifications and Statements of Attainment issued by any other Registered Training Organisation. To apply, you’ll need to provide verifiable evidence — such as a statement of results — and advise the college of your acquired or pending qualifications before or during the enrolment process.

sections.heading: Overview

blocks.text: Australia continues to be one of the world’s most preferred destinations for vocational education, offering internationally recognised qualifications that prepare students for real workplace success. According to the Australian Government, hundreds of thousands of international students choose Australia every year for its high-quality education system, while the Vocational Education and Training (VET) sector provides nationally recognised qualifications that meet industry needs. If you are planning to study business or management, the Diploma of Leadership and Management Australia is one of the most practical and career-focused qualifications available.

At Austra College, we help students find the right study pathway based on their academic background and career aspirations. If you are still exploring your options, visit our Business Courses page to compare available programs or explore our Student Services page to understand the support available before and after your arrival in Australia.

To ensure you choose a nationally recognised qualification, always verify course information through the Australian Skills Quality Authority (ASQA) , Training.gov.au, and the CRICOS register. International students should also review the latest student visa requirements published by the Department of Home Affairs before applying.

sections.heading: What is the BSB50420 Diploma of Leadership and Management?

blocks.text: The BSB50420 Diploma of Leadership and Management is a nationally recognised vocational qualification designed for individuals who want to develop practical leadership, communication, operational planning, and team management skills.

Unlike traditional academic degrees that focus heavily on theory, this qualification combines practical learning with real business scenarios. Students learn how to manage teams, improve workplace performance, solve organisational challenges, and communicate effectively across different business environments.
The qualification is suitable for aspiring managers, supervisors, team leaders, entrepreneurs, and professionals who want to take the next step in their careers.
As a nationally recognised qualification listed on Training.gov.au, graduates gain skills that are valued across Australia in multiple industries.

sections.heading: Why Choose the Diploma of Leadership and Management Australia?

blocks.text: Many international students choose this qualification because it develops practical workplace skills while opening pathways to further education and employment. Some of the key benefits include:
Nationally recognised qualification
Practical industry-focused curriculum
Strong leadership and communication training
Flexible career opportunities across different industries
Pathway to advanced qualifications
Suitable for students from diverse educational backgrounds
Delivered by CRICOS-registered education providers
Since leadership and management skills are transferable across industries, graduates are not restricted to one specific career field.

sections.heading: Why Choose a Leadership and Management Course VET?

blocks.text: A leadership and management course VET focuses on practical learning rather than purely theoretical knowledge. Students participate in:
Workplace simulations

Professional presentations

This practical approach helps students become job-ready while developing confidence in managing people, projects, and business operations. Australian VET qualifications are designed in consultation with industry, ensuring graduates develop skills employers are looking for.
